title: Prevalence and effect of misinformation on Twitter during the COVID-19 pandemic: A mixed-methods social media analysis
screen_reason: Quantitative component assesses the top 10 most-shared news articles on Twitter for each of three COVID-19 topics across four 3-month windows (114 article links). Article TITLES were checked against evidence-based sources; 30/114 (26.3%) contained misinformation, with topic-level shares of 47.5% (alternative treatments), 20.0% (transmission) and 8.8% (vaccines). The paper also reports, per topic, the number of Twitter shares generated by misinformation articles out of total shares, which yields exact part/whole engagement-weighted shares.

estimates.country: Global (authors state they included global data and did not restrict to a specific population; limitation notes most posts were from North America and Europe, English only)
estimates.platform: Twitter (most-shared news article links, identified via BuzzSumo)
estimates.date: 1 April 2020 - 1 April 2021, in four 3-month windows (Apr-Jul 2020; Jul-Oct 2020; Oct 2020-Jan 2021; Jan-Apr 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-shared COVID-19 news article links on Twitter whose titles contained misinformation (all three topics pooled)
estimates.value_raw: In total, 30 news articles (26.3%) contained misinformation; 30/114 article links
estimates.denominator: 114 English-language news article links shared through tweets (top 10 most-shared per topic per window; 40 alternative treatments + 40 transmission + 34 vaccines; 120 slots intended but only 4 vaccine articles existed in the first window)
estimates.definition: An article entered the numerator if the claims made in its TITLE were judged to contain misinformation on comparison with evidence-based and reputable sources (government agencies, international organizations, peer-reviewed literature). Articles that could not be assessed from the title alone, or for which credible comparison sources were insufficient, were left in the denominator as non-misinformation
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation refers to the creation and spread of false or inaccurate information"
estimates.source_quote: In total, 30 news articles (26.3%) contained misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Each article was independently assessed twice for misinformation by two researchers, by comparative analysis against evidence-based and reputable sources (government agencies, international organizations, peer-reviewed scientific literature). The paper states explicitly: 'Inter-rater reliability was not assessed in this study.'
estimates.moderator_quote: Boolean operators and keywords for each topic of interest were employed to obtain the top 10 shared articles for each of the three topics at four chosen time intervals (n = 120 articles).
estimates.notes: POOLED ROW - the three topic rows below decompose exactly this figure (19 + 8 + 3 = 30 of 40 + 40 + 34 = 114); do not pool the pooled row together with the topic rows. Two serious quality caveats: (a) only article TITLES were assessed, not article bodies ('only the titles of the top 10 circulating news articles were assessed'); (b) 20 of 114 articles (7 treatments, 9 transmission, 4 vaccines) 'could not be assessed based on the title alone or due to insufficient credible sources' yet stay in the denominator, so this is a lower bound. Inter-rater reliability explicitly not assessed. Time series (four windows, Figure 1) collapsed to the paper's own across-period total. year set to 2020 as the modal collection year; the window spans April 2020-April 2021.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) An overall engagement-weighted misinformation share across all three topics is NOT extracted: it would require summing numerators and denominators across the three separately sampled corpora, which is a cross-category sum forbidden by R8. (2) 'Could not be assessed' rates (17.5% of treatment articles, 22.5% of transmission, 11.8% of vaccines) are measurement-failure rates, not misinformation shares. They matter for interpretation - because these articles stay in the denominator, every CONTENT row here is a LOWER BOUND - but a 'misinformation among assessable articles' figure (e.g. 19/33) would be a computed value and is not kept. (3) Per-time-period prevalences are plotted in Figure 1 only; the figure's values are not in the text, so the four-window series is collapsed to the paper's across-period totals. Directional statements only: treatments and transmission misinformation decreased over time, vaccines increased; vaccine misinformation appeared only in windows 3 and 4; transmission misinformation was concentrated in windows 1 (n=3) and 3 (n=3). (4) The whole qualitative component (240 tweets, 80 per topic, March 8-22 2021, coded as positive/neutral/negative perceptions of vaccine acceptance, mask adherence and lockdown compliance) reports NO share of tweets in any category - only narrative descriptions and example tweets (Table 3) - so it yields no row; it is also attitude coding, not misinformation exposure. (5) Country: coded Global on the authors' own statement that global data were included; the limitation that 'most social media posts collected were from users in North America and Europe' is qualitative and does not license a country code.

rob.design: Concurrent mixed-methods secondary analysis of public social-media data (no ethics approval required). QUANTITATIVE: BuzzSumo used to retrieve the top 10 most-shared English-language news articles on Twitter for each of three Boolean keyword topics (alternative COVID-19 treatments, transmission, vaccines) in each of four 3-month windows from 1 April 2020 to 1 April 2021; duplicates excluded; 114 of an intended 120 links obtained (only 4 vaccine articles existed in window 1). Misinformation was judged from ARTICLE TITLES ONLY, by comparative analysis against government agencies, international organizations and peer-reviewed literature; each article was assessed twice, independently, by two researchers, but INTER-RATER RELIABILITY WAS NOT ASSESSED (stated verbatim). Engagements (likes, shares, comments) were summed per article, period and topic. QUALITATIVE: 240 tweets (80 per topic) archived with TAGS over 8-22 March 2021, open-coded in sequence by two researchers; retweets, ads, link-only and non-English tweets excluded; no counts reported. Author-stated limitations: title-only assessment, English-only and mostly North American/European posts, TAGS 2-week retrieval limit, text-only data, single platform, no causal inference.
